en: An arrogant brute,
A master of swift assaults,
A stalwart who ravaged the earth,
The wrathful infidel,
The hero of potent venom,
Rode onto the field with a roar,
Straining like a blue tiger,
Girded with blue-gray steel,
Before the hero's menace,
Most men hid themselves,
His splendid bearing became a terror,
His eyes dimmed as strength filled him,
He screamed like a scourge,
Calling for someone to ride out alone:
“Come, your lion favored by fortune!
Come, your stalwart hero, fully armed!
Come, you who level the great spear!
Come, you who deliver into my hands
The punishment of whoever advances!
Come, your lion of surpassing courage!
Come, your ready wrestler and hero!
Come, you who stand beneath the banner!
Come, satisfy the itching place,
And thrust your spear without delay!
Come, your warrior and your lion!
Come, your wrestler and your hero!
Come, you who slash and wage battle!
Come, you who finish all you seize
And tear their ribs apart!
Let the few remaining and the many come!
Let your hero come and leave no regrets!
My wrath has risen; I stand rigid,
I desire only to level my spear,
Whoever meets me shall die,
I shall put your women in black headdresses,
I shall vanquish your great ones,
I shall devour your weak,
Your wrestlers and your heroes—
I shall gouge out their eyes,
I who ruin nations and slaughter peoples,
I am Sarybay!
When I charge in fury,
I shall richly grease my sword,
I shall chew up the whole world, sparing none,
Yesterday you sorely provoked my rage,
I shall lay waste to all, leaving not a hair,
My wrath has risen; I stand rigid,
If you come out to clash, I transform,
If you enter the field, I go mad,
I mangle whoever crosses me,
I am the black scourge itself,
Gnawing whoever I encounter,
I am the black eye of the scourge,
I embody every kind of horror,
When I devour, blood cannot sate me,
When I grapple, I spare no life,
I am the black scourge itself,
You cannot go on swaggering about,
Stirring up quarrels for sport,
Why do you not restrain your courage?
How many troops have you killed?
Why have you roused this madness?
I shall overturn your burden,
My raging frenzy has seized me,
I shall not spare one of you,
I shall enslave your people,
Such is the nature of battle,
I shall destroy your lives,
I shall exhaust every stratagem,
I shall turn aside
Your flowing river,
I shall break your backs,
I shall chill your breath,
If you are a hero, be one like me—
I shall knock the wind from you,
I shall drench your banner in blood,
I shall silence your clamor at one stroke,
If I toy with you, you will not recover,
Your lumbering frenzy will not subside,
I shall master your clever one,
I shall defeat your champion,
The sly Kyrgyz have grown insolent—
I shall settle all their accounts together,
I shall slaughter them, sparing not a hair,
You have provoked my rage, you wretches,
I shall kill many of your lions!”
Thus spoke Sarybay,
Taking the form of a night-devouring fiend,
The swine spoke with a roar,
Shouting menacingly,
“Come here to confront me!” he cried,
Calling out the heroes,
His eyes like the hollows of a lake,
As though he would suck dry any soul he saw,
Such was his splendid appearance,
Whichever way you looked at him,
He seemed like a dragon lying coiled,
Ready to reduce the whole wide world to dust,
Driving it before him and swallowing it,
Tall of stature and broad of shoulder,
A monstrous wrestler, a great affliction,
Dark and formidable, fit to face a hero,
He taunted the army and called them out,
Standing there and speaking these words,
When you looked at Sarybay,
He seemed to constrict the age itself,
And make precious heads grow old,
As though in this wretched world
He alone would become its master,
As though he would drive and devour
The entire wide world,
Crushing every feeble soul,
The madman fancied himself
Ready to slaughter them and unleash conflict,
As though, with none left to oppose him,
He would become the master
Of all eighteen thousand worlds,
Such was the madman's state,
As though he would shatter the whole world,
Driving all before him and slaughtering them.
With his hair bristling wildly,
With his mane like a famished boar’s,
Thundering like hell itself,
Making mountains crumble beneath his surging force,
The infidel began his roaring,
And the deep black earth below
Seemed ready to break apart.
When he raged in fury,
His pine-like spear
And the roar he gave
Seemed his only stratagem.
Such was Sarybai’s nature:
Where a torrent ran, no water could pass;
Where flame swept, no ember could pass;
When a musket fired, no bullet could pierce him.
An end-time terror, mighty in venom,
His fury swelled whenever he roared;
Like a fire-engulfed flood,
He advanced alone,
A sovereign power of might,
For life is fashioned in every kind.
Whoever faced him with leveled spear,
Stripped five times over by his dread renown,
Turned back without confronting him.
Not only speaking men, but beasts
Panicked beneath his gaze.
Before the infidel’s dread presence,
Not even five thousand troops could stand;
Against the infidel’s terrible force,
No age of men could endure.
No man could answer the infidel
And meet him in combat;
No man could harry him with strife,
Draw near, and overcome him.
No brave man could withstand
His formidable courage.
Though all the peoples of the world surrounded him,
No man could defeat the villain.
Of towering courage and stony heart,
Great indeed was Sarybai;
Thus he raised a mighty tumult.
What regret is left to those who saw?
A warrior indeed was Sarybai;
Thus he raised a mighty conflict.
His fame brought devastation;
He raged and wrought havoc,
And the dog’s violence only grew.
When he strode onto the field and roared,
The forest fell and the willows shattered,
Mountains broke and eyes flashed;
No man could advance against him,
Courage fled and eyes stared wide.
Sarybai stood there raging,
Armed with all his weapons,
Upon the broad plain of Kosh-Töbö.
The people clashed amid a great outcry
Upon the field of battle;
Those who boasted of strength and valor
Lost heart and bowed,
While my champions and lions
Despaired of their wretched lives.
“Such is Sarybai;
He has waged the battle relentlessly.
Whenever the madman moves,
He slaughters multitudes of us.
Against this infidel Sarybai,
Can any man’s strength prevail?
Can even a lion’s fang pierce him?
For us to regain peace,
When will this swine ever die?
He has emptied the land and slaughtered the people;
On what blessed day will dawn break,
And when will God deliver us?”
Pining away in anguish,
The people despaired of life;
The savagery of the boar
Who devastated the nation was revealed.
Wildly exulting, he roared,
“Who will come out to single combat?”
And called forth in fury.
He urged on Too-Kyzyl beneath him,
Making the horse stride ponderously;
A grievous sight even to contemplate,
He threw the whole world into panic.
Raising the clamor of bloody slaughter,
Enshrouding the wondrous mountains in haze,
Your infidel, vast as Mount Kap,
Armed himself and came out to fight.
The infidel Khan Sarybai
Shot and hacked through the battle;
The people panicked, unable to prevail,
And despaired of their mortal lives;
Unable to find their bearings, they fled.
When strong men’s backs were broken,
When he slaughtered all who faced him,
They fought but could not prevail;
Six times before this
They had battled without defeating him.
The poor people merely watched;
Whenever Sarybai entered the field,
The nation cried out in anguish,
Despairing of their fly-like lives.
Their courage failed and they cringed,
Wondering how many souls would be slaughtered;
Their sight dimmed and their eyes bulged
Whenever Sarybai entered the fray.
The people wailed in misery,
And languished beneath their punishment.
Against Sarybai’s venom
No human strength prevailed;
He was like the wrath of the true God,
The very image of a death-defying man,
Fierce in anger and mighty in venom,
With the black eyes of a fiend.
The people despaired of life;
Already timid, the poor folk
Grew sallow as in a wasting sickness.
They spoke together in whispers;
The poor people were crushed,
Unable to find their bearings.
Against the infidel warrior Sarybai,
Not one soul could venture forth.
The whole world was stricken with fear,
And every counsel was exhausted;
All the warriors stood helpless,
Wondering whence this monster’s son,
This infidel, had sprung.
“Which broad-necked young warrior
Will go out to face him alone?
Who will dare encounter him in battle?
Who can fathom the measure
Of this thousandfold courageous scourge?
Who, experienced and wise among the people,
Will go against this infidel Sarybai
With keen judgment?
Which great champion called a lion
